title: What is the CAP theorem and how does it guide design decisions?
description: Consistency, availability, partition tolerance: why networks force trade-offs, and how the real design axes are CP, AP, and partition handling.

data.text: **Question:** What is the CAP theorem and how does it guide design decisions?

CAP says a distributed system can guarantee at most two of three properties **during a network partition**: **Consistency** (every read sees the latest write), **Availability** (every request gets a response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system survives node/network failure). Since partitions *will* happen, the real choice is **CP** (refuse or block some requests to stay consistent — e.g., a relational store with synchronous replication, ZooKeeper, etcd) or **AP** (answer anyway, possibly with stale data — e.g., Cassandra, DNS). Good design guidance: decide per data store and per operation what happens during a partition, and remember the deeper axes — **latency vs consistency** (strong consistency costs round trips) and **conflict resolution** (how you merge divergent writes) — matter more in daily work than the CAP label itself.

**The three properties, precisely:**
- **Consistency (linearizability)**: all nodes return the same, most recent value — a single logical system state
- **Availability**: every non-failing node responds to every request (no 'try later')
- **Partition tolerance**: messages between nodes can be lost/delayed arbitrarily (a real network) and the system keeps running

**Why the choice only exists during partitions:** outside a partition you can have all three (consensus protocols like Raft give C+A when the network is healthy). The theorem bites when a link breaks: do you answer with possibly-stale data (AP) or refuse/block until consistency is restored (CP)?

**CP in practice:**
- Leader-based stores (PostgreSQL sync replication, MongoDB, etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka for topic metadata)
- During a leader election/partition, writes fail or wait — correctness over responsiveness
- Right for: money, inventory counts, unique-ID enforcement, coordination

**AP in practice:**
- Multi-leader/Dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB in some modes), DNS, CDNs
- Writes proceed on both sides; conflicts resolved by last-writer-wins, vectors, or app-level merge
- Right for: shopping carts, feeds, telemetry, caches — data where "latest wins" or client merge is acceptable

**The finer axes (what interviewers really want):**
- **PACELC** extends CAP: else (no partition) the axis is **Latency vs Consistency** — even healthy systems choose between fast async replication and slow sync
- **Conflict handling**: LWW loses data silently; CRDTs merge provably; app-level reconciliation is honest but costly
- **Per-operation granularity**: a system can be AP for profile updates and CP for payment authorization — no single letter describes an architecture
- Don't use CAP as 'we chose AP so we don't need replicas' — replication and partition strategy are separate, explicit decisions

data.title: Choosing per data store, with partition behavior spelled out
data.code:
Inventory reservation (CP - correctness over uptime)
  during partition: writes to unavailable region fail fast (503 + retry-after)
  why: overselling costs money; blocking a purchase is acceptable

Shopping cart (AP - availability over immediate consistency)
  during partition: each region accepts cart edits; merge on heal
  why: a merged cart is recoverable; a rejected add-to-cart is lost revenue

Leader election / config (CP)
  during partition: minority side stops serving writes entirely
  why: split-brain config is worse than downtime

Feed generation (AP with bounded staleness)
  during partition: serve last-known feed, tag 'may be out of date'
  why: a slightly stale feed beats an error page

Even outside CAP, specify latency-consistency per call (PACELC):
  read-your-own-writes: session stickiness + async replica wait (ELC trade)
  money movement: sync replication wait (accept higher latency)

data.title: CAP is a partition-day tool, not an architecture label
data.text: Saying 'our system is AP' only answers what happens when a link breaks. The questions that shape daily design are: how stale may each read be? which writes must be serialized? what does the client see during the 3 a.m. partition? Answer those per data store and operation — the letters follow.

items: Treating CAP as 'pick two of three any time' — the trade-off exists only during a partition
Labeling an entire system CP or AP instead of deciding per data store and operation
Choosing AP for money or inventory and discovering the conflict-resolution bill later
Ignoring PACELC: healthy-network latency-consistency choices get forgotten
Assuming AP means no replication strategy — conflicts still need a merge design
Using CAP to justify not engineering partition behavior at all
What does PACELC add to CAP, and where does latency appear?
How would you merge two cart writes made during a partition?
Why is DNS a classic AP system?
How do consensus protocols (Raft) reconcile with CAP?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: During a partition: CP refuses/blocks for consistency; AP answers possibly-stale
Partitions are inevitable, so the real choice is CP vs AP behavior
PACELC adds the healthy-network latency-vs-consistency axis
Decide per data store and per operation; specify conflict handling explicitly
data.takeaway: CAP is the question you answer on the worst day (partition): which requests do you refuse so the data stays true?
